Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.
slides: Welcome back, and now three groups. Sometimes the exam adds a third group, and asks how many must be in all three.

slides.say: At least how many are in all three groups? Let's turn the question around. Who is not in all three? Anyone who misses at least one group.
So we count the people who miss each group, as if they're all different people. That's the most people who can miss something. Everyone else must be in all three.
at: Everyone else must be in all three

slides.say: Let's see it in numbers. There are ten friends. Eight like tea, nine like coffee, and seven like juice.
Two don't like tea, one doesn't like coffee, and three don't like juice. Two plus one plus three is six.
So at most six friends miss something. The other ten minus six, four friends, must like all three.

It's the same idea as with two groups. Fifteen students, ten in art and nine in drama. Five miss art, and six miss drama. Five plus six is eleven, so at least fifteen minus eleven, four are in both. The same four as the sum minus the total.
at: fifteen minus eleven, four are in both

slides.say: Now careful. What if the people who miss a group add up to more than the total? There are fifty readers. Thirty read fiction, thirty-five read history, and twenty-five read science.
Twenty miss fiction, fifteen miss history, and twenty-five miss science. Twenty plus fifteen plus twenty-five is sixty. That's more than fifty readers.
Fifty minus sixty would be negative. But a number of people can't be negative. So, just like with two groups, the smallest is zero.
Is zero really possible? Here's one way. Fifteen read fiction and history. Fifteen read fiction and science. Ten read history and science. And ten read only history.
Fiction is fifteen plus fifteen, thirty. History is fifteen plus ten plus ten, thirty-five. Science is fifteen plus ten, twenty-five. That's fifty readers, and nobody reads all three.
And the most in all three? The people in all three are inside every group. So it can't be more than the smallest group. Here that's twenty-five.
One more case. Sometimes they also tell us how many each pair of groups shares. Here are three clubs. Forty students are in chess, thirty-five in drama, and thirty in music.
Twelve are in both chess and drama. Nine are in both chess and music. And fifteen are in both drama and music. At most how many are in all three?
at: Twelve are in both chess and drama

slides.say: Someone in all three clubs is also in every pair. So the all-three group fits inside each pair. It can't be bigger than the smallest pair, nine.
So the most is nine, not thirty. When we know only the groups, the smallest group is the limit. When the pairs are given, the smallest pair is the limit.

And the least? Here it can be zero. In chess, twelve plus nine is twenty-one, and that fits in forty. In drama, twelve plus fifteen is twenty-seven, and that fits in thirty-five. In music, nine plus fifteen is twenty-four, and that fits in thirty. So the pairs can all be different people.
at: and that fits in thirty. So

slides.say: So here it's from zero to nine.
Now a question with exact numbers. A school play had three performances, with nine actors in each performance.
at: A school play had three performances

slides.say: Three actors were in all three performances, and six actors were in exactly two. How many actors were in exactly one performance?
at: Three actors were in all three

slides.say: Let's draw the three performances as three circles. Each circle holds the nine actors of one performance.
The circles make three kinds of regions. In the middle are the actors in all three performances.
at: In the middle are the actors

slides.say: Where just two circles overlap, outside the middle, are the actors in exactly two.
And the outer part of each circle is for the actors in exactly one performance. That's what we're looking for.
at: And the outer part of each circle

slides: We don't know how the six actors in exactly two are split among the three pairs. And we don't need it. So instead of people, we count appearances. Every time an actor plays in one performance, that's one appearance.

slides.say: There are three performances, with nine actors in each. So three times nine is twenty-seven appearances.
Now, how many appearances does each actor make? An actor in exactly one performance appears once. An actor in exactly two appears twice. And an actor in all three appears three times.
at: An actor in exactly one performance appears once
And an actor in all three

slides: Remember, with two groups, we took both away twice, because the people in both are counted in each group. Here it's the same idea, with three groups.

slides.say: The three actors in all three performances make three times three, nine appearances.
The six actors in exactly two make six times two, twelve appearances.
Together that's nine plus twelve, twenty-one appearances. Twenty-seven minus twenty-one leaves six appearances.
Who made those six appearances? Only the actors in exactly one performance are left, and each of them appears once. So six actors were in exactly one performance.
at: So six actors were in exactly one

slides.say: So when we add up the groups, we count appearances, not people. How many different actors were there? Three plus six plus six is fifteen. So there were fifteen actors, not twenty-seven.

Here we know every group's size, and the counts in all three and exactly two. So we can subtract their appearances to find exactly one. We need those other counts too, not just the group sizes. Counting appearances doesn't tell us which pair each actor was in, and we don't need that.
